Introduction

Explicit estimates for the distribution of primes assuming the Riemann Hypothesis has been widely investigated. A good starting point is Schoenfeld's thorough article [14] which is the second part of a similarly impressive paper by Rosser and Schoenfeld [12]. Büthe has proved explicit results assuming the partial Riemann Hypothesis, namely, that the Riemann Hypothesis holds up to some height [4]. The aim of this article is to treat primes in arithmetic progressions assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.
Let now π(x; q, a) = p≤x p≡a mod q 1, where gcd(a, q) = 1, compute the number of primes up to x which are congruent to a modulo q. By de la Vallée Poussin [10] π(x; q, a) ∼ x ϕ(q) log x .

Furthermore, we can also consider the term π(x; q, a) assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), indeed that if L(s, χ) = 0, where L is a Dirichlet L-function and s is not a negative real number, then ℜs = 1/2. It is known (see e.g. [6,Chapters 19 and 20]) that assuming the GRH, we have (1) π(x; q, a) = Li(x) ϕ(q)
+ O √ x log x where Li(x) = x 2 dt log t ∼ x log x .
